Abstract
              
                Background
                Shared decision making (SDM) is a systematic approach aimed at improving patient involvement in preference-sensitive health care decisions. Choosing between surgical or non-surgical treatment for lumbar disc herniation, can be difficult as the evidence of a superior treatment is unclear, which makes it a preference-sensitive decision. The objectives of this study was therefore to assess the degree of SDM and afterwards to develop and test a patient decision aid (PtDA) to support SDM during the clinical encounter between surgeon and patient, when patients choose between surgical and non-surgical treatment for Lumbar disc herniation (LDH).
              
              
                Methods
                The study was conducted in four steps.

                    
                      
                      
                        Assessment of the extent to which SDM was practiced in the spine clinic.
                      
                    
                    
                      
                      
                        Development of a PtDA to support SDM.
                      
                    
                    
                      
                      
                        Testing its usability and acceptability amongst potential users (patients).
                      
                    
                    
                      
                      
                        Pilot-test of its usability in the clinical setting.
                      
                    
                  
              
              
                Results
                Results from our small baseline study (n = 40) showed that between a third and two-thirds of the patients reported not being fully engaged in a shared decision. A pre-designed template (BESLUTNINGSHJÆLPER™) was adapted to support the decision about whether or not to have surgery for LDH. Testing the prototype with patients led to minor refinements. A subsequent pilot test of its usability in a clinical setting achieved positive responses from both patients and clinicians.
              
              
                Conclusion
                Our baseline study demonstrated that SDM was not universally practiced in the clinic. The PtDA we have developed was rated as acceptable and usable by both patients and clinicians for helping those with LDH choose between surgical or non- surgical treatment. This tool now requires further testing to assess its effectiveness.

Abstract

Background
Shared decision making (SDM) is a structured method designed to increase patient participation in preference-sensitive health care choices. Deciding between surgical and non-surgical treatment for lumbar disc herniation can be challenging because the evidence for a superior option is unclear, making it a preference-sensitive decision. The aim of this study was therefore to evaluate the extent of SDM and then develop and test a patient decision aid (PtDA) to support SDM during the clinical encounter between surgeon and patient when patients choose between surgical and non-surgical treatment for Lumbar disc herniation (LDH).

Methods
The study was carried out in four steps.

Assessment of how extensively SDM was practiced in the spine clinic.
Development of a PtDA to support SDM.
Testing its usability and acceptability among potential users (patients).
Pilot testing its usability in the clinical setting.

Results
Findings from our small baseline study (n = 40) showed that between one-third and two-thirds of patients reported not being fully involved in shared decision making. A pre-designed template (BESLUTNINGSHJÆLPER™) was adapted to support the decision about whether to have surgery for LDH. Testing the prototype with patients resulted in minor refinements. A later pilot test of its usability in a clinical setting produced positive feedback from both patients and clinicians.

Conclusion
Our baseline study showed that SDM was not consistently practiced in the clinic. The PtDA we developed was judged acceptable and usable by both patients and clinicians to help those with LDH choose between surgical and non-surgical treatment. Further testing is now needed to evaluate its effectiveness.
